The work we automated was the training. Nobody planned a replacement.

5 min read
Just now

--

Before a pilot can fly for a US airline, the law requires 1,500 hours of flight time.
Not talent. Not a test score. Hours. Aviation learned, at great cost, that judgment in the cockpit cannot be taught in a classroom. It must be accumulated hour by hour and in the seat.
Aviation wrote this rule into law but, business never did. We assumed the hours would always be there, because the junior work would always be there.
For me this year, that assumption quietly broke.
Here is a test before we continue. Name the task that trained your judgment early in your career. The financial model you built at midnight. The hundred documents you reviewed. The report you rewrote four times.
Now check: does that task still exist in your company?
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: AI generatedAnatomy ⓵ The routine work was never just work
The common view of junior work is that it is low-value task and AI can now does it faster. Everyone moves up. This is presented as pure gain.
But look closer at what those tasks actually produced.

• The analyst who built financial models by hand learned where numbers hide their lies.

• The junior lawyer who read a thousand contracts learned what “normal” looks like. So the abnormal one jumped out instantly, years later, as a partner.

• The young engineer who debugged other people’s code learned how systems fail.
The output of junior work was never the spreadsheet, contracts or software. The output was the judgment of the person who made it. The task was the apprenticeship. We just never called it that — so when the task disappeared, no alarm sounded.
Action: Run an apprenticeship audit. List the five tasks that built your current leadership team’s judgment. Mark which of them still exist for juniors today.
Anatomy ⓶ The deletion is now measurable
This is no longer a prediction.

• A Stanford study of payroll records covering millions of workers found that employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations fell by roughly 13 to 16 percent in relative terms, while older workers in the same occupations were unaffected. Entry-level jobs with low AI exposure did not decline either. The effect is specific: young people, in exactly the roles AI can do.

• A Harvard working paper found the same pattern inside companies. At firms adopting generative AI, junior hiring contracted while senior employment kept growing. The mechanism was quiet: juniors who left were simply not replaced. The researchers gave it a name : “seniority-biased technological change.” In big technology companies, new-graduate hiring fell 25 percent in a single year.
Honest caution: some economists note that junior hiring began slowing before modern AI arrived, and other forces also play a role. The trend has more than one source. But the pattern inside AI-adopting firms is specific and consistent , no company should bet its leadership pipeline on the optimistic reading.
Action: Measure your own funnel. Not just junior headcount but junior decision exposure. How many real decisions does a early-year employee participate in today, compared with five years ago?
Anatomy ⓷ The counter-argument deserves respect. And a condition.
“But juniors will learn faster with AI.” This is half right. The half matters.
When AI passed human chess ability, experts predicted the death of the game. The opposite happened. Engines became the training partners. Every serious young player now studies with an AI stronger than any human coach. And this era has produced the youngest elite players in history including Gukesh Dommaraju of India, who became the youngest world chess champion at eighteen.
AI did not end chess careers. It became the best training tool the game ever had.
But note the condition: chess redesigned training around the machine, deliberately. The engine is a sparring partner, not a substitute. The young player still plays every game.
Most companies are doing the opposite. The AI does the work. The junior watches. Watching builds no rigor hours.
Action: Convert saved junior hours into deliberate practice. Let juniors shadow live decisions: they write their own recommendation first, then compare it with what the senior team decided — and with what actually happened.
Anatomy ⓸ Rebuild the path around decisions, not tasks
For decades, careers were structured by task volume. Do enough financial models, become a manager. Review enough contracts, become a partner. Task volume was how we counted the hours.
If AI absorbs the tasks, the structure must change: progression measured by decision exposure, not task completion.
You can do this by asking junior members to write their position before every major review. The senior decision is then compared with theirs, openly. It costs ten minutes. It is the cheapest flight time we can offer in Business.
Action: Create one metric e.g. a decision repetitions per junior per quarter. Report it like any pipeline metric. What gets measured gets protected.
The Synthesis
This month I have written about Jugdement: that it is the scarce asset when analysis becomes free; that it cannot be outsourced to systems trained to agree; that it must update cheaply as the world changes.
All of it depends on one assumption that judgment keeps being produced.
Judgment has a supply chain. It runs on repetitions, the way a pilot’s judgment runs on hours. We have just automated the repetitions, and celebrated the efficiency.
The companies that win the next decade will do both: automate the work and rebuild the apprenticeship on purpose. Not because it is kind. Because their 2035 leadership team is sitting in the junior seats today — or nowhere.
The question: What was the task that made you? And would today’s version of you ever get to do it?
